To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. IR injury is mediated by the interplay between the innate and the adaptive immunity; 2. The innate immunity is activated by the release of endogenous danger signals such as heme, heat shock proteins and extracellular ATP;

(1) the liver is an important organ for the generation of pro‐ and anti‐inflammatory mediators, (2) these mediators are crucial for the development of hepatic IR injury, (3) the heme oxygenases and the CXC chemokine systems are key mediators of the inflammatory response in hepatic IR, (4) Toll‐like receptors are important regulators of the inflammatory response and (5) apoptosis is a crucial mechanism of cell death in hepatic IR

(1) heme oxygenase (HO‐)1, a key mediator of the anti‐inflammatory effects of heme oxygenase, plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of IR injury; (2) the CXC chemokine, macrophage inflammatory protein‐2, is a crucial mediator of neutrophil‐mediated hepatic injury in IR injury; (3) toll‐like receptors, in particular, toll‐like receptor‐4, play a critical role
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms underlying hepatic IR injury with the ultimate goal of developing novel strategies to prevent or ameliorate this important clinical problem.
understanding how the liver copes with the challenges of ischemia and reperfusion, and how we might manipulate the response in order to improve clinical outcomes.
understanding the molecular and cellular basis of hepatic inflammation, and developing novel therapies to improve outcomes in patients undergoing liver surgery and transplantation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hepatic IR injury is a complex and dynamic process involving a multitude of different cells, mediators and mechanisms.
hepatic IR is complex, and the pathogenic mechanisms are multifactorial, involving the activation of a number of different signalling pathways and cell types.
the pathogenesis of hepatic ischemia re‐perfusion injury is complex, involving multiple pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the good (heme oxygenase‐1) and bad (chemokines) can be deadly (apoptosis) in the liver after IR injury.
the pathogenic mechanisms of hepatic IR injury are complex and multifaceted.
there are many good and bad things about IR injury and the good things are bad and the bad things are deadly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IR‐induced inflammation and hepatocyte injury are interdependent, and that the two are regulated by common signalling pathways.
IR injury is a complex process that is not only dependent on the severity of the initial ischemic insult but also the nature of the reperfusion milieu.
there are many different ways in which IR injury occurs and the mechanisms of injury vary depending on the type of injury.
